seasons.review_body: Beyond Evil aired on JTBC from February 19 to April 10, 2021, sweeping the 57th Baeksang Arts Awards with Best Drama, Best Screenplay, and Best Actor for Shin Ha-kyun. The series places two officers, the demoted, eccentric Dong-sik and the elite Seoul transplant Joo-won, in a provincial town where a 20-year-old serial murder case reopens. Writer Kim Su-jin builds the thriller around mutual suspicion: each detective privately suspects the other is the killer. The structure stays ambiguously balanced and the show does not resolve its moral questions cleanly. IMDb audience scores settle at 8.1. The series draws inspiration from the Hwaseong murders case without fictionality turning exploitative. Shin Ha-kyun and Yeo Jin-goo sustain a two-lead tension that is rare in procedural drama.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Beyond Evil S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The call comes early and oddly plain. Oh Ji Hun says it is nothing, then says **Lee Dong Sik** needs to be fetched quickly. That contradiction becomes the pilot’s operating system. Every scene claims to be routine until it changes category: a café dispute, an assault report, a missing dementia patient, a dinner with too much control in the room. "Episode 1" works because it treats procedure as pressure. The law does not clarify the mystery here. It makes the mystery more dangerous.

## The Law Arrives Before the Truth

The first sharp move is how quickly the episode converts mood into paperwork. Dong Sik is singing at the live café, then the customer dispute escalates and pulls him out of that ordinary space. By, the matter has a police shape: an assault or attempted assault case at Salon de Manyang, with Dong Sik tied to it. The hour does not start by clearing or condemning him. It starts by asking how fast a room can turn from local mess into case file.

That is why the arrest beat lands. When the police declare everyone in the room under arrest for multiple crimes, the scene changes category. Local friction becomes criminal procedure. The charge basis later connects the café salon incident to gambling and abetting, which gives the sequence a useful ugliness. Dong Sik is not framed as a clean hero entering a dirty world. He is already standing inside a room where the law can grab everyone.

The craft choice works because the pilot refuses a neat first impression. Dong Sik wants to avoid trouble while policing allegations, yet the allegations keep tightening around him. His job should put him above the chaos. Instead, his authority feels contaminated by proximity. That is the first proper Beyond Evil hook: in Manyang, procedure does not wash the dirt off. It identifies who has dirt under the nails.

## Han Ju Won Turns Procedure Into a Blade

**Han Ju Won** enters the hour through rules, and those rules quickly become aggression. The missing-person discussion is thick with legal limits, especially around what counts for a child missing report. The chief insists on reporting. Ju Won pushes into the restriction. He wants proper procedure, yet the dossier’s central contradiction shows the deeper move: he uses legal limits to deny or redirect a missing report, then later interrogates the cold-case connection as if the case is already actionable.

That contradiction is the pilot’s best writing engine. Ju Won does not break procedure by ignoring it. He weaponizes it by applying it with selective force. In a weaker pilot, the new inspector would be pure order entering a corrupt village. Here, order has an edge. His legal knowledge matters less than what he wants the law to do for him.

The scene gives the episode its density, and that density cuts two ways. The legal conversation gives texture to the missing-person thread, planting how classification may affect the investigation later. It also slows the hour into dialogue-to-dialogue procedure. That is mostly productive, because the pilot is building a world where definitions matter. Still, the sequence asks for attention before the emotional stakes are fully locked in. The show trusts the codebook early. Sometimes the codebook makes the room colder than it needs to be.

## A Missing Man, a Controlled Town

The search for Mr. Bang changes the scale without changing the method. Dong Sik is trying to locate the missing dementia patient. The case is smaller than the cold-case shadow, but it tells the same story in miniature: a person goes missing, procedure activates, and the human problem risks becoming an operational problem.

The control beat matters. The instruction about not making reports on a personal phone from now on gives the sequence grounded police texture. There is no glamour here, no chase rhythm. The scene is about repeatable systems, who controls information, and how mistakes are prevented. That kind of detail is where the pilot shows its confidence. It lets a missing dementia patient case teach the rules of the town before the larger mystery takes over.

Dong Sik benefits from this stretch because it complicates the earlier Salon de Manyang mess. He is tied to suspicion, but he also does the work. He searches. He responds. He operates inside the community rather than above it. The episode does not clear him through competence, which is the smarter choice. Competence can hide as much as it reveals.

The Mr. Bang material is the pilot’s quietest flex. It makes Manyang feel less like a backdrop for one murder question and more like a place where every report has a memory attached. The town comes into focus through who gets called, who gets controlled, and who is allowed to decide what counts as missing.

## Dinner Sings the Wrong Song

The dinner scene with **Oh Ji Hwa** and Han Ju Won is a tense social machine. Ji Hwa tells Ju Won to memorize and sing properly, and the instruction sounds comic until it does not. In a pilot obsessed with procedure, even dinner has rules. Learn the song. Perform correctly. Do not expose how little you belong.

That is a clean character beat for Ju Won. He has been positioned through legal precision, but here the pressure is cultural and interpersonal. He can know the law and still fail the room. The episode uses singing as a test of compliance, which neatly echoes Dong Sik’s café opening. Songs in this hour are surveillance with melody.

The scene also lets the show shift gears without leaving its thesis. Earlier, authority arrives through arrest and reporting requirements. Here, authority arrives through etiquette. Ji Hwa’s control of the table gives the dinner a sharp little hierarchy, and Ju Won’s outsider status becomes more visible. He is asking questions in Manyang, while Manyang is testing whether he can stand there without disturbing the ritual.

The limitation is that the pilot’s midsection can feel packed with procedural and social instruction. The density is intentional, but it leaves less room for one emotional beat to breathe. The pauses in the hour help the authority announcements land, yet the writing still stacks mechanisms faster than it reveals feeling. The trade works because the final interrogation gives those mechanisms a target.

## The Sister Question Cuts Through the Case File

The ending is where the pilot reveals what it has been doing. Inspector Han states that **Lee Yu Yeon** is Dong Sik’s sister, then asks whether she was killed. The question ties identity, cold case, and suspicion into one direct strike. It also reframes the earlier procedural care. Ju Won’s concern with missing-person classification is not detached neatness. It belongs to a larger push toward an old wound.

That is why the final confrontation works. It does not introduce a new genre. It sharpens the genre already present. The café arrest, the missing report debate, the search for Mr. Bang, the controlled dinner: each scene has been about the terms under which a person can be named, accused, reported, or remembered. Lee Yu Yeon turns that pattern into the core mystery.

The episode’s strongest choice is that it never lets Dong Sik sit comfortably on either side of the line. He is an officer. He is tied to allegations. He is the brother of the cold-case figure. He is also the person being challenged through that connection. The pilot understands that suspicion is more interesting when it attaches to someone useful, familiar, and already compromised by the room he stands in.

"Episode 1" is a procedural pilot with a serrated edge. Its weakness is early heaviness, especially when legal explanation bunches up before the emotional hook fully opens. Its strength is architecture. Every mundane rule points toward the final question.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a strong, controlled pilot that builds dread through systems rather than spectacle. The hour’s best idea is simple: in Manyang, paperwork is never neutral. A missing-person rule, a mass arrest, a phone-report instruction, and a dinner performance all measure power. The episode can be dense, and a few stretches lean hard on procedural explanation before the characters fully warm the frame. Still, the structure pays off when Han Ju Won turns Lee Yu Yeon’s identity into an accusation against Dong Sik. That last question gives the pilot its bite and plants the season’s central pressure around Dong Sik, Ju Won, and the cold case that has returned to the center of town.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 15
episode_reviews.review_body: Beyond Evil's penultimate episode arrives as the series' most dramatically pressurised hour - the accumulated weight of fourteen episodes of mutual suspicion collapsing into its most direct confrontation. Joo-won's moral framework, built on a faith in institutional law and a certainty about who he is, has been incrementally dismantled across the season by everything Dong-sik represents about what justice actually requires in a place the system has failed. Episode 15 is where the dismantling reaches completion. Kim Su-jin's script delivers the confrontation the thriller's structure has been promising without releasing the tension early - the episode ends not in resolution but in the kind of suspended moral ambiguity that makes the finale necessary rather than merely concluding. The two lead performances here match the material at the level of the series' Baeksang sweep.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Penultimate episode where the accumulated suspicion reaches its breaking point. The series' most dramatically pressurised hour, with Joo-won's moral framework finally failing under the weight of what Dong-sik represents.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dong-sik speaks to Joo-won with a warmth that is either genuine or the show's most unsettling misdirection - the scene divides viewers to this day.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.review_body: Beyond Evil's finale resolves its central question with the moral precision the series earned across sixteen episodes. Writer Kim Su-jin's decision about what the truth is - and what the show's two leads do with it - is simultaneously satisfying and uncomfortable in exactly the way the thriller's structure demanded. The resolution does not simplify either man or retroactively make either's suspicion of the other incorrect; it arrives at an understanding that acknowledges the weight of what both carried. The final address between Dong-sik and Joo-won is the episode's performance peak: Shin Ha-kyun's register in the scene is fatherly and strange and precise about the distance that remains between them even as the confrontation concludes. Beyond Evil swept the 57th Baeksang Arts Awards with Best Drama, Best Screenplay, and Best Actor, and the finale is the concentrated version of what the series earned those recognitions for.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers a resolution that feels satisfying without being clean. The show's refusal to simplify its two leads pays off in a closing hour that circles back to the town, the case, and the costs both men paid.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Dong-sik's final address to Joo-won - fatherly, strange, quietly devastating.
